name: The Ayutthaya Kingdom
title: Social Hierarchy of the Ayutthaya Kingdom: From King to Slave

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You are hailed as Lord of the Land and a bodhisattva, and in theory every man’s service is yours; but any prince of your clan may claim your throne, and your generals have seized it before.
tiers.kid: The king of Ayutthaya was called Lord of the Land, and people spoke to him in a special royal language.
tiers.rise: No settled law fixed the succession. The king often named a preferred successor as uparaja, but any man of the royal clan could claim the throne by defeating his rivals: in the 17th century, as one study puts it, “the method of royal succession at Ayutthaya … was battle”. Officials took it too: the Kalahom Prasat Thong in 1629, and Phetracha, Narai’s elephant commander, in 1688.
tiers.why: From the 17th century the king of Ayutthaya was an absolute monarch with a semi-religious standing.

tiers.name: Princes of the royal clan
tiers.you: You are a son of the king by one of his many wives and must live in the capital under his eye; if you are named uparaja you may reign one day, should you outlast your brothers and uncles.
tiers.kid: The king’s sons and brothers lived at court, and one of them was chosen to be the next king.
tiers.rise: Princes were born to the rank. Thai tradition favoured brothers over sons, but nearly every succession was contested, and the losers often died: Prince Sisin, the late king’s brother, was captured and executed in 1628, and King Chai was deposed and executed by his uncle in 1656.
tiers.why: The king’s kin stood above every official.

tiers.name: Officials and lords
tiers.you: You hold a title and rice lands from the king and command your own registered phrai, whom you call up for war and royal works; in a struggle for the throne your men can help make a king, or cost you your head.
tiers.kid: Each noble in Ayutthaya had a number that showed his rank, and he led the men who worked and fought for the king.
tiers.rise: Offices were mostly inherited, but the king could raise new men, and foreigners often rose high: the Greek adventurer Constantine Phaulkon became Narai’s prime minister. A fall could be fatal. Purges of officials followed conflicts with the king, and Phaulkon was executed in 1688.
tiers.why: A service nobility of a few thousand men governed the kingdom.

tiers.name: Monks and court Brahmins
tiers.you: You have joined the sangha, free of the labour service your lord once called you to; the rice the peasants have left over after their own needs and their taxes goes to support temples like yours.
tiers.kid: Buddhist monks lived in temples, and any man, rich or poor, could become a monk.
tiers.rise: Any man could enter the sangha, and many phrai did so to escape their lords’ control. A monk could also leave it: in 1760 the people of the capital urged Uthumphon, a former king living as a monk, to lead its defence against the Burmese.
tiers.why: Theravada Buddhism was the kingdom’s main religion, and its monastic community, the sangha, stood partly outside the sakdina order, for men of every class could join it.

tiers.name: Chinese and foreign communities
tiers.you: You are a Chinese trader in Ayutthaya, free of the labour service that binds the king’s own subjects, and you may travel and trade wherever you please in the kingdom.
tiers.kid: Traders from China, Japan, Persia and Europe lived in Ayutthaya, and some of them served as the king’s guards.
tiers.rise: Foreigners rose with a king’s favour and fell with it: Prasat Thong had Yamada Nagamasa assassinated in 1630 and banished the Japanese, and a Makassar revolt failed in 1686. The Chinese grew with the rice trade to China in the late 17th and 18th centuries.
tiers.why: Ayutthaya was a great port, and its foreign communities had a place of their own.

tiers.name: Commoners
tiers.term: phrai luang, phrai som, phrai suay
tiers.you: Your name is on your lord’s register; for half of each year you dig canals or work his fields, and when war comes you march with his men, unless you bribe the recruiting officer or slip away into the forest.
tiers.kid: Most people in Ayutthaya were rice farmers, and every man had to work for the king or a lord for part of each year.
tiers.rise: A phrai could become a monk, or sell himself as a slave to another lord, who compensated his old one. Many simply escaped: they fled into the forests or bribed conscription officers, and as trade grew more of them slipped away to farm on their own.
tiers.why: Every free man was registered as a phrai under a lord, a system Ramathibodi II (r. 1491–1529) made general.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were taken in war, or sold yourself to clear a debt, and now belong to a master who may set you to work in his gardens or let you earn your own living if you pay him a few ticals a year.
tiers.kid: Some people in Ayutthaya were slaves who belonged to a master, often because they were captured in war or owed money.
tiers.rise: Slavery came by capture, debt, sale or birth. It was abolished in stages from 1874 to 1905, under King Chulalongkorn, and legally ended only in 1915.
tiers.why: Slaves, that (from the Pali dasa), formed the lowest rank, with a sakdina of 5.
